items.prompt:
Read these two texts.

Text 1: Apples grow on trees. They come in red, green, and yellow. Apples are a healthy fruit to eat.

Text 2: Rosie the apple was red and round. She lived on the tallest branch. One windy day, she tumbled off and rolled all the way to the farmer's basket.

Which text is fiction and which is informational? How do you know?
items.answer: Text 1 is informational. It gives real facts about apples. Text 2 is fiction. It has a made-up character (Rosie the apple) who does things a real apple cannot do, like living on a branch and rolling to a basket on purpose.

steps: Text 1 has no characters and gives true facts: apples grow on trees, come in colors, are healthy. Text 2 has a named character (Rosie), a setting (the tallest branch), and events. Apples cannot really think or be named. These are signs of fiction.

items.prompt:
Read this text below.

I am a little raindrop,
Falling from the sky.
I splash on rooftops, puddles, grass,
As I go rushing by!

Give two features that tell you this is a poem, not a story.
items.answer: Feature 1: It rhymes (sky/by). Feature 2: It is written in short lines, not paragraphs.

steps: 'Sky' and 'by' rhyme at the end of lines. This is a poetry feature. The text is also arranged in short lines, not in sentences organized into paragraphs. These two features identify it as a poem.

items.prompt: A book called 'How Sharks Hunt' has chapters, headings, and real photos of sharks. Is this book most likely fiction, a poem, or an informational book? Explain.
items.answer: It is most likely an informational book. Chapters, headings, and real photos are features of books that teach real facts. The title also tells you it is about how sharks really hunt.

steps: Chapters and headings are text features used in informational books to organize facts. Real photos show real things. The title says 'how sharks hunt,' which suggests it teaches true information. Poetry and fiction do not usually include headings or real photos.

items.prompt: A book has a character named Benny Bear who goes to school, makes friends, and learns to share. Is this book most likely fiction or informational? Explain.
items.answer: It is most likely fiction. It has a made-up character (Benny Bear). Bears do not go to school in real life. The book tells a made-up story with characters, a setting, and events.

steps: Bears do not go to school or make friends the way the story describes. This means the events are made up. Made-up characters doing made-up things is the definition of fiction. This book is a story, not a book of real bear facts.

items.prompt:
Read this text below.

Oceans cover more than half of the Earth. They are home to millions of animals. The biggest ocean is the Pacific Ocean.

And read this text below.

The Ocean Queen had pearls in her hair.
She ruled every fish, every whale, every wave.
With a flick of her tail, she could quiet the storm.
Or raise up the tide and have sailors cave.

What is the first text? What is the second text? What makes them different?
items.answer: The first text is informational. It gives real facts about oceans. The second text is a poem (or fiction). It has a made-up character (the Ocean Queen), rhymes, and events that cannot happen in real life. One teaches facts and the other tells a story through poetic language.

steps: First text: facts (more than half of Earth, millions of animals, Pacific Ocean). No characters. Informational. Second text: Ocean Queen is a made-up character. There are rhymes. The events (quieting storms, raising tides) are not real. It reads as a poem with story elements. Both are about the ocean but in completely different ways.

items.prompt: Can a poem contain facts about real things, like animals or weather? Explain your thinking.
items.answer: Yes, a poem can mention real things. But what makes it a poem is not the content but how it is written, with rhyme, rhythm, or short lines. A poem about the weather can include real facts, but it is still a poem because of the way it is structured.

steps: Text type is determined by how something is written, not just what it is about. A poem can include true information. A poem about frogs can have real facts about frogs, but if it has rhymes and short lines, it is still a poem. The structure and style determine the type, not the topic.

items.prompt:
Read this text below.

The caterpillar wraps itself in a cocoon. Inside, it slowly changes. After some weeks, it comes out as a butterfly.

A student says this could be the beginning of a fiction story because caterpillars really do change into butterflies. Is the student right?
items.answer: The student makes a fair point, but this text reads as informational because it gives real facts without any characters or story events. If it had a named caterpillar and described its feelings or adventures, it would be fiction. The facts alone do not make it fiction.

steps: Real events can appear in both fiction and informational texts. What matters is whether the text has characters, a plot, and made-up elements. This text just states facts in plain sentences. There are no named characters or events. Without those elements, it reads as informational, even though the event (transformation) is real.

items.prompt:
Read this text below.

Worms help the soil.
They dig deep tunnels below.
The roots love their neighbors,
And together they grow.

Is this a poem or an informational text? It mentions real facts about worms. How does the way it is written help you decide?
items.answer: This is a poem. Even though it mentions real facts (worms dig tunnels, roots benefit), the way it is written shows it is a poem: short lines, a rhythm, and figurative language ('the roots love their neighbors'). Informational texts do not use that kind of language.

steps: The content involves real information, but the form is poetic. Short lines and rhythm are poem features. 'The roots love their neighbors' is figurative language, not a plain fact. Informational texts state facts directly and plainly. This text gives information in a poetic way, which makes it a poem, not an informational text.

items.prompt: List two things a fiction story has that an informational book usually does not have.
items.answer: Two things: (1) Characters, people or animals doing things in a made-up story. (2) A plot with a problem and solution.

steps: Fiction stories have characters (made-up people or animals) and a plot (a sequence of events with a problem and resolution). Informational books focus on facts and do not have characters or a plot.

items.prompt: List two things an informational book has that a fiction story usually does not have.
items.answer: Two things: (1) Real facts that are true about the world. (2) Features like headings, photos, or diagrams to organize information.

steps: Informational texts have real facts (not made up) and often use text features like headings, bold words, captions, photos, or diagrams. Fiction stories do not usually have these features.

items.prompt:
Read this text below.

Little Leo loved lightning bugs.
He chased them through the yard.
He caught one in a jar of glass,
But let it go, not hard.

Is this a story or a poem? Give two reasons from the text.
items.answer: This is a poem. Reason 1: It rhymes (yard/hard). Reason 2: It is written in short lines, not paragraphs.

steps: 'Yard' and 'hard' rhyme. The lines are short and arranged in a stanza. Even though there is a mini-story about Leo and the lightning bug, the way it is written (rhyme and short lines) makes it a poem.

items.prompt: Would you find the sentence 'Penguins are birds that cannot fly' in a fiction story or an informational book? Explain.
items.answer: You would most likely find it in an informational book. It is a plain statement of a real fact about penguins. Fiction stories would show a penguin doing things in a story, not state facts in plain sentences.

steps: The sentence is written as a fact, not as part of a story. It names a real animal and states something true about it. This is the style of informational writing. In a fiction story, we would meet a penguin named something, see it trying to fly, fail, and have an adventure instead.

items.prompt:
Read this text below.

Sam's class got a book about spiders. The book had real photos and chapters. It explained how spiders spin webs and catch insects.

Is the book Sam's class read a fiction story or an informational book? How do you know?
items.answer: The book is an informational book. It has real photos, chapters, and explains how spiders really behave. These are all features of informational texts.

steps: Real photos show real things, not made-up events. Chapters and explanations of real behavior (spinning webs, catching insects) are features of informational books. If it were fiction, it would have spider characters doing made-up things.

items.prompt: Your friend says: 'Any book with animals in it is fiction.' Do you agree? Explain.
items.answer: No, I disagree. Animals can appear in both fiction and informational books. A fiction book might have a talking rabbit on an adventure. An informational book might give real facts about rabbits. The type of text depends on whether the events are made up or real.

steps: Animals appear in both types of text. In fiction, animals may talk, think, or have made-up adventures. In informational books, animals are described with true facts about their behavior, habitat, and bodies. The presence of animals alone does not tell you the text type.

items.prompt:
Read this text below.

Fly, little bird, fly so high,
Where clouds are soft and winds blow by.
Sing your song for all to hear,
Your sweet notes fill the sky with cheer.

And read this text below.

A little bird sat on Aisha's windowsill every morning. She named it Sunny. One day, Sunny did not come. Aisha waited, but the windowsill stayed empty.

Which is a poem and which is a fiction story? Name one feature from each.
items.answer: The first text is a poem. Feature: it rhymes (high/by and hear/cheer). The second text is a fiction story. Feature: it has characters (Aisha and Sunny), a setting (the windowsill), and events (Sunny stops coming).

steps: First text: 'high/by' and 'hear/cheer' rhyme. Short lines. No plot. Poem. Second text: Aisha is a character. Sunny is a named bird. There are events and an emotional ending. Fiction story.
